title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Weeks 13-16. Very rapid growth, the placenta fully takes over, coordinated limb and slow eye movements, breathing movements, recognisable external genitalia, ovaries with primordial follicles.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Weeks 17-20. Quickening (movements felt by the mother), lanugo and eyebrows, skin covered by vernix caseosa, brown fat for heat production, testes begin to descend.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Weeks 21-25. Sucking and rapid eye movements, type II cells begin making surfactant; a baby born now can survive but with a high risk of neurodevelopmental disability.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Weeks 26-29. Viable: lungs and CNS can maintain breathing and temperature; the spleen hands blood production over to the bone marrow by about 28 weeks.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Weeks 30-38. Pupillary light reflex, pink smooth skin, fat on the limbs, testes fully descended; from 32 weeks babies usually do well; birth weight about 2.5-3.5 kg.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Weeks 9-12. Low-set ears, fused eyelids, primary ossification centres, the physiological hernia returns, liver, pancreas and kidneys start working, swallowing begins; genitalia still look alike.
Embryo: fertilisation to end of week 8 (organogenesis). Fetus: week 9 to birth (growth and maturation).
Length: months 3-5. Weight: months 8-9.
Fused eyelids, low ears, ossification, physiological hernia returns, organs start working, swallowing.
Quickening, lanugo, eyebrows, vernix caseosa, brown fat, testes begin to descend.
Surfactant, REM, sucking (21-25); viability, marrow haematopoiesis by 28 weeks (26-29).
Full term 37-40 weeks; preterm < 37; post-maturity > 42 weeks.
LBW < 2500 g; SGA < 10th percentile for age; IUGR: not reaching genetic growth potential.
Maternal chronic disease, smoking, alcohol, twins, poor uteroplacental flow, genetics.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Intraembryonic coelom. Cavity that forms in the lateral mesoderm; its link with the extraembryonic coelom narrows, and it gives the pericardial, pleural and peritoneal cavities.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Trilaminar disc. Flat three-layered disc lying between the amniotic cavity and the umbilical vesicle before folding.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Head fold. Brings the primordial heart, pericardial coelom and oropharyngeal membrane ventrally; the septum transversum ends up caudal to the heart; part of the yolk sac becomes the foregut.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lateral folds. Form the lateral and ventral body walls; the midgut stays connected to the umbilical vesicle by the omphaloenteric (vitelline) duct.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Tail fold. Brings the connecting stalk and allantois to the ventral surface; the primitive streak now lies caudal to the cloacal membrane; part of the endoderm becomes the hindgut.
Skeleton, skeletal and visceral muscle, dermis, connective tissue, urogenital system, serous membranes, heart, blood, spleen, adrenal cortex.
First segmentation; date the embryo; form axial skeleton, its muscles and dermis.
Median (head and tail folds) and horizontal (lateral folds).
Heart, pericardial coelom and oropharyngeal membrane move ventrally; septum transversum caudal to heart; foregut.
Connecting stalk and allantois ventral; primitive streak caudal to the cloacal membrane; hindgut.
Body walls; midgut with vitelline duct; intraembryonic coelom separated; amnion expands.
Yolk sac (3-8 wk), liver (6 wk-birth), spleen (10-28 wk), bone marrow (from 18 wk).
Any agent causing abnormal development; e.g. alcohol (FAS), cocaine, heroin; most harmful during weeks 3-8.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Oogonia. Female germ cells that multiply by mitosis only in the fetal ovary; there is no renewable stem cell pool after birth.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Primary oocyte. Enters meiosis I in fetal life and stops at prophase I (diplotene) inside a primordial follicle, sometimes for decades, until just before ovulation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Spermatogonia. Stem cells by the basal lamina of the seminiferous tubule; type A keep dividing, type B go on to become primary spermatocytes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Secondary oocyte. Formed with the first polar body just before ovulation; stops at metaphase II and completes meiosis II only if fertilised.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Primary spermatocyte. Largest germ cell (2n chromosomes, 4N DNA); a long prophase I (about 22 days) then meiosis I gives two short-lived secondary spermatocytes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Spermatids and spermiogenesis. Meiosis II gives four haploid spermatids that transform, without division, into spermatozoa: acrosome, condensed nucleus, flagellum, loss of cytoplasm.
Mitosis: 2 identical diploid cells. Meiosis: 2 divisions, crossing-over, homologues then chromatids separate, 4 haploid cells.
Spermatogonia (A stem, B committed) → primary spermatocyte → secondary spermatocyte → spermatid → spermatozoon.
Transformation of spermatids into sperm without division: acrosome, nuclear condensation, flagellum, loss of cytoplasm.
Only before birth, by mitosis; they then become primary oocytes arrested in prophase I.
Primordial (flat cells) → primary (cuboidal, zona pellucida) → secondary (theca, vesicles) → Graafian (antrum, cumulus).
Prophase I from fetal life to ovulation; metaphase II from ovulation until fertilisation.
Removal of the seminal-plasma coat in the female tract (5-7 h), giving hyperactive motility and allowing the acrosome reaction.
Diploid number restored, sex determined, cleavage starts.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Neural crest. Cells at the edges of the folds migrate widely: spinal, cranial and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, meninges, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, facial bones, odontoblasts, heart septum.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Notochord. Cells from the primitive node migrate cranially to the prechordal plate; the notochord defines the axis, gives rigidity, induces the neural plate and leaves the nucleus pulposus.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Neural plate. Thickened ectoderm over the notochord; its edges rise as neural folds around a neural groove.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Neural tube. The folds fuse into the tube that forms the brain and spinal cord; the cranial neuropore closes around day 25 and the caudal one around day 28.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Primitive streak. First sign of gastrulation, on the caudal epiblast; its cranial end is the primitive node with the pit. It fixes the cranio-caudal, dorso-ventral and left-right axes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Trilaminar disc. Epiblast cells invaginate through the streak: some replace the hypoblast (endoderm), others form mesoderm between the layers; the remaining epiblast is ectoderm.
Germinal (fertilisation to implantation), embryonic (to week 8), fetal (week 9 to birth).
Week 3 formation of three germ layers from the epiblast through the primitive streak; starts morphogenesis.
Primitive groove, node (cranial) and pit; it sets the body axes.
First replace the hypoblast as endoderm, then form mesoderm; remaining epiblast becomes ectoderm.
Axis, rigidity, induction of the neural plate and axial skeleton, nucleus pulposus.
Neural plate → neural folds and groove → neural tube; neuropores close ~day 25 and ~28.
Ganglia (cranial, spinal, autonomic), Schwann cells, meninges, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, facial bones, odontoblasts, heart septum.
Anencephaly (cranial); spina bifida occulta, meningocele, myelomeningocele (caudal).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Foregut buds. Hepatic diverticulum (liver, gallbladder, bile ducts) and dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds appear in week 4 from the duodenum.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Foregut. Pharynx, lower respiratory tract, oesophagus, stomach and the duodenum down to the bile duct opening; supplied by the coeliac trunk.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hindgut. Distal third of the transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, upper anal canal, and the epithelium of the bladder and most of the urethra; inferior mesenteric artery.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Midgut. From the distal duodenum to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon (jejunum, ileum, caecum, appendix, ascending colon); supplied by the superior mesenteric artery.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Midgut rotation. The midgut loop herniates into the cord in week 6, rotates 270° anticlockwise around the SMA and returns by week 10, caecum last.
Stomodeum, pharynx, foregut, midgut, hindgut, cloaca; oropharyngeal and cloacal membranes at the ends.
Pharynx, lower respiratory tract, oesophagus, stomach, proximal duodenum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas.
Grows (greater curvature), descends C2→T11, tilts, rotates 90° clockwise, shifts left.

title: Three week-4 buds from the duodenum?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: Three week-4 buds from the duodenum?
body.back: Hepatic diverticulum, ventral pancreatic bud, dorsal pancreatic bud.
Haematopoiesis week 6-birth, albumin week 5, bile week 12, glycogen late.
Herniation week 6; 270° anticlockwise (90° out, 180° on return); back by week 10; caecum descends last.
2% of people, ~2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, ~2 inches long, 2:1 male.
Omphalocele: at the umbilicus, covered by membrane, often other anomalies. Gastroschisis: beside the umbilicus, uncovered.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Two cavities. The amniotic cavity forms within the epiblast (future water bag); the primary then secondary umbilical vesicle lies under the hypoblast.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Embryoblast. The inner cell mass becomes a bilaminar disc: epiblast (dorsal, towards the amnion) and hypoblast (ventral, towards the yolk sac).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lacunae. Spaces in the syncytiotrophoblast fill with maternal blood from eroded sinusoids: the start of the uteroplacental circulation; primary villi follow.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Extraembryonic mesoderm. Splits into somatic and splanchnic layers around the chorionic cavity; the connecting stalk remains the only link between embryo and trophoblast.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Trophoblast. The outer cell mass: cytotrophoblast makes new cells; the syncytiotrophoblast, a multinucleated mass, invades the endometrium and secretes β-hCG.
Sperm preparation (capacitation, acrosome reaction), binding and fusion, cortical reaction.
Diploid number restored, sex determined, cleavage started.
Morula: solid ball of blastomeres. Blastocyst: cavity, trophoblast and embryoblast.
Cyto: mitotic layer making new cells. Syncytio: multinucleated, invades endometrium, secretes β-hCG.
Keeps the corpus luteum secreting oestrogen and progesterone; detected in pregnancy tests.
Endometrial cells store nutrients and create an immunosuppressive environment for the blastocyst.
2 trophoblast layers, 2 embryoblast layers (epiblast, hypoblast), 2 cavities, 2 layers of extraembryonic mesoderm.
The only link between embryo and trophoblast at the end of week 2; becomes the umbilical cord.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Alpha-fetoprotein. Fetal glycoprotein (liver, yolk sac, gut), peaking in fetal serum at ~14 weeks; high in open neural tube and abdominal wall defects, low in maternal serum in Down syndrome.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Amniocentesis. Amniotic fluid taken at 15-18 weeks for chromosomes, neural tube defects and genetic disorders; indications include maternal age, family or parental anomalies, previous spina bifida, inborn errors.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cordocentesis. Fetal blood drawn from the umbilical cord after 18 weeks for genetic, blood and infectious conditions.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chorionic villus sampling. Biopsy of trophoblast at 10-12 weeks for karyotype and genetic tests; earlier results than amniocentesis but a slightly higher miscarriage risk.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Spectrophotometric study. Analysis of amniotic fluid pigments to grade the severity of haemolytic disease of the newborn.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ultrasound. Cheap, available and without known adverse effects: confirms pregnancy and site, size, twins, placenta position and malformations (mid-trimester), growth and position (last trimester).
Amnion, umbilical vesicle (yolk sac), allantois, chorion.
~30 mL at 10 weeks, 450 mL at 20 weeks, 800-1000 mL at 37 weeks.
Cushion, prevents adhesions, allows movement, homeostasis, lung development, prenatal diagnosis, cervical dilation.
Poly > 2 L: can't swallow (GI, CNS anomalies). Oligo < 500 mL: placental insufficiency, urinary anomalies; pulmonary hypoplasia.
Nutrition (weeks 2-3), primordial germ cells (week 3), blood islands (weeks 3-6), primitive gut (week 4).
Urachus → median umbilical ligament.
CVS 10-12 weeks; amniocentesis 15-18 weeks; cordocentesis after 18 weeks.
High: open neural tube or abdominal wall defect. Low maternal serum: Down syndrome and other chromosomal defects.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Endometrial veins. Drain maternal blood from the intervillous space to the uterine veins and back to the mother's heart.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Intervillous space. Formed from fused syncytiotrophoblast lacunae; the mature placenta holds about 150 mL of maternal blood, replaced three to four times a minute.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Spiral arteries. About 80-100 maternal endometrial arteries spurt blood into the intervillous space.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Umbilical arteries. Two arteries carrying poorly oxygenated blood from the fetus to the chorionic arteries and the villous capillaries.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Umbilical vein. A single vein bringing oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chorionic villi. Fetal capillaries inside villi bathed in maternal blood; exchange happens by diffusion across the placental membrane.

title: Origin and functions of placenta and membranes?
subject: subj:embryo1

body.front: Origin and functions of placenta and membranes?
body.back: Trophoblast; protection, nutrition and excretion, endocrine support, immunological barrier.
Fetal: chorion frondosum. Maternal: decidua basalis. Chorion laeve is the smooth, villus-free part.
Starts week 3; vascular network week 4; villi all over sac week 8; fully formed week 12.
Uterine → spiral arteries → intervillous space (~150 mL, 3-4×/min) → endometrial and uterine veins.
2 umbilical arteries → chorionic arteries → villous capillaries → chorionic veins → 1 umbilical vein.
2 arteries, 1 vein, Wharton's jelly, allantois remnant, vitelline duct remnant.
Protein: hCG, placental lactogen, thyrotropin, corticotropin. Steroid: progesterone, oestrogens.
Dizygotic: always DCDA. Monozygotic: DCDA (early), MCDA (~65%), MCMA (rare, late).
